concepts.name: Origins and Historical Context of Company School Painting
key_dimensions: Emergence during British East India Company rule (18th–19th century) and the colonial administrative context
Transition from Mughal/regional court patronage to European mercantile patronage
Role of the decline of Mughal Empire in displacing court artists towards Company patronage
Distinction between 'Company School' as a pan-Indian phenomenon vs. regional court traditions

concepts.name: Patronage Structure and Commissioning Dynamics
key_dimensions: European patrons: Company officials, British residents, surgeons, botanists, and travellers as primary commissioners
Shift from royal/aristocratic patronage to individual European and middle-class British patrons
Role of the East India Company in commissioning botanical, zoological, and ethnographic documentation
Contrast with Mughal patronage system: collective court workshop vs. individual artist-patron relationship

concepts.name: Stylistic Synthesis: Indian and European Techniques
key_dimensions: Adoption of European conventions: perspective, shading, chiaroscuro, and naturalism by Indian artists
Retention of Indian elements: flat colour areas, fine line work, and decorative treatment in certain works
Use of Western watercolour on paper vs. traditional Indian gouache (opaque watercolour) on wasli paper
UPSC trap: Company School is a hybrid style, NOT purely European or purely Indian — examiners test this overlap

concepts.name: Key Regional Schools within Company Painting
key_dimensions: Murshidabad School: earliest centre, Bengal; patronised by Nawabs and Company officials
Patna/Patna Qalam (Bihar): distinctive for depicting artisans, trades, and everyday life with realism
Delhi School: influenced by late Mughal miniature tradition; associated with artists like Ghulam Ali Khan
Tanjore and Madras schools: South Indian Company painting with distinct treatment of flora/fauna and festivals

concepts.name: Patna Qalam (Patna School) — Distinctive Identity
key_dimensions: Also called 'Patna School' or 'Bihar School'; flourished from late 18th to early 20th century
Subject matter: documentation of local trades, crafts, festivals, costumes, and occupational castes
Artists from Patna: Sewak Ram, Hulas Lal, Shiva Lal — notable names for UPSC
UPSC trap: Patna Qalam is often confused with Mughal miniature; key difference is subject focus on commoners and trades

concepts.name: Subject Matter and Thematic Categories
key_dimensions: Natural history documentation: botanical illustrations, birds, animals, and fish (scientific utility)
Ethnographic studies: castes, occupations, festivals, costumes, and social ceremonies ('castes and trades' albums)
Architectural and landscape depictions: Indian monuments, ruins, and landscapes for European audiences
Portrait painting of Indian nobles, Company officials, and soldiers

concepts.name: Botanical and Natural History Illustration — Scientific Dimension
key_dimensions: Company commissioned Indian artists for systematic botanical surveys (e.g., William Roxburgh's flora documentation at Calcutta Botanical Garden)
Artists like Vishnupersaud (Vishnu Prasad) worked under Roxburgh producing thousands of botanical plates
Distinction: These works served scientific/documentary purposes, unlike decorative court miniatures
Connection to broader colonial project of cataloguing Indian flora and fauna for economic exploitation

concepts.name: Role of European Artists and Their Influence on Indian Painters
key_dimensions: William Hodges and the Daniells (Thomas and William) — early European artists in India who inspired hybrid style
Johann Zoffany, George Chinnery — European painters who worked in India and trained or influenced local artists
Transfer of techniques: Indian artists learned perspective and oil painting by observing/copying European works
UPSC distinction: European artists working in India ≠ Company School; Company School refers specifically to Indian artists working for European patrons

concepts.name: Albums and 'Bazaar Paintings' — Popular Commercial Dimension
key_dimensions: 'Souvenir' paintings and albums sold to Europeans departing India — proto-tourist art
Bazaar paintings: cheaper, more standardised versions produced for general European market vs. commissioned fine works
Standardised subjects: trades, gods, festivals packaged in sets/albums
Debate: artistic merit vs. commercial commodification — examines how colonialism altered artistic purpose

concepts.name: Medium, Materials, and Format Innovations
key_dimensions: Shift from traditional wasli (layered paper) to European machine-made paper and ivory
Adoption of transparent watercolour (European) alongside traditional opaque gouache
Shift in format: from vertical manuscript-style pages to horizontal landscape compositions for European taste
Ivory miniatures: a specialised product for European clientele, different from Mughal paper miniatures

concepts.name: Decline of Company School Painting
key_dimensions: Introduction of photography in India (1840s–1850s) as primary cause of decline — replaced documentary function
Transfer of power from East India Company to British Crown (1858) changed patronage dynamics
Establishment of European-style art schools (e.g., Bombay School of Art 1857, Madras School 1850) redirected artistic training
Rise of Bengal School (Swadeshi-era) as a conscious rejection of both Company style and academic European realism

concepts.name: Comparison: Company School vs. Mughal Miniature Tradition
key_dimensions: Patronage: Imperial Mughal court vs. individual European patrons
Subject: Imperial grandeur, religious, and courtly scenes vs. everyday life, natural history, trades
Style: Flattened Mughal perspective vs. adoption of Western three-dimensional perspective in Company works
UPSC trap: Company School artists were OFTEN trained in Mughal tradition — it is evolution/adaptation, not a completely separate lineage

concepts.name: Company School vs. Bengal School — Contrasting Colonial Responses
key_dimensions: Company School: Indian artists adapting TO European aesthetics for colonial patronage (accommodation)
Bengal School (Abanindranath Tagore et al.): conscious rejection of European realism, revival of Indian/Asian traditions (resistance)
Temporal relationship: Company School (18th–19th c.) precedes Bengal School (late 19th–early 20th c.)
UPSC trap: Both emerged in colonial context but represent opposite artistic responses to colonialism

concepts.name: Notable Artists of the Company School
key_dimensions: Ghulam Ali Khan (Delhi): documented Mughal court remnants and Delhi architecture for British patrons
Sewak Ram and Hulas Lal (Patna): leading artists of Patna Qalam school
Shaikh Muhammad Amir of Karraya (Calcutta): known for equestrian portraits and domestic scenes
Vishnupersaud (Calcutta): prolific botanical illustrator for William Roxburgh — UPSC frequently pairs artist with patron/institution

concepts.name: Institutional Connections: Company, Surveys, and Art Documentation
key_dimensions: Geological Survey of India, Botanical Survey, and Archaeological documentation employed Company-style artists
Asiatic Society of Bengal (founded 1784) as intellectual backdrop encouraging documentation of Indian culture
Connection to Orientalism: Company paintings as visual instruments of colonial knowledge production
Role of Fort William College, Calcutta in fostering cross-cultural interaction between European officers and Indian artists

concepts.name: Company School and the Documentation of Indian Castes and Occupations
key_dimensions: 'Seventy-two Specimens of Castes in India' type albums — systematic ethnographic visual catalogues
Colonial gaze: these works reflect European fascination with 'exotic' Indian social structure
Artists depicted washermen, weavers, potters, musicians, dancers — occupational taxonomy in visual form
Critical perspective: Such works served colonial administrative knowledge (census-type classification) — relevant to polity overlap

concepts.name: Geographical Spread and Urban Centres of Company Painting
key_dimensions: Major centres: Calcutta (Bengal Presidency), Patna (Bihar), Delhi, Lucknow, Murshidabad, Tanjore, Madras, Pune
Calcutta as the most commercially active centre due to its status as colonial capital
Lucknow: influenced by Nawabi culture; Company artists depicted both European and Indo-Nawabi subjects
UPSC trap: Different centres had distinct stylistic flavours — 'Company School' is an umbrella term, not a uniform style

concepts.name: Company School Paintings as Historical Sources
key_dimensions: Value as primary sources for social history: costumes, architecture, occupations, and festivals of 18th–19th century India
Limitations as historical sources: European patron's gaze shaped what was depicted and what was omitted
Use in reconstructing urban history of colonial cities like Calcutta, Delhi, and Madras
Overlap with GS-1 History: These paintings are evidence for understanding colonial society, deindustrialisation effects on artisans

concepts.name: Legacy and Revival Interest in Company School Paintings
key_dimensions: Major collections held in: Victoria and Albert Museum (London), British Library, National Museum (New Delhi), Ashmolean Museum
Growing academic and auction market interest — Company paintings fetching high prices internationally
Reassessment from post-colonial perspective: from 'hybrid curiosity' to recognition as legitimate artistic tradition
Influence on understanding of how Indian artists negotiated colonial modernity — relevant for cultural history essays

concepts.name: Company School and Its Relationship to Traditional Indian Regional Styles
key_dimensions: Rajput and Pahari painters largely unaffected by Company influence — contrast with plains/court artists
Kalighat painting (Calcutta, 19th c.) emerged contemporaneously — comparison: both serve new urban/middle-class audiences but with different aesthetics
Tanjore painting tradition continued alongside Company commissions in South India — parallel existence
UPSC trap: Company School influence was NOT pan-Indian uniformly — regional styles showed varying degrees of absorption of European techniques
